items.title: Is North Korea holding back on sending Russia more troops?
items.summary: A North Korean troop buildup Ukraine warned about months ago has yet to materialize, even as strategic cooperation continues. Analysts say Pyongyang is balancing its ties with Moscow and Beijing.
items.body:
https://p.dw.com/p/5PoFF

Prefer DW on Google

North Korean leader Kim Jong Un commemorated troops killed in Ukraine earlier this yearImage: KCNA/REUTERS

Advertisement

Over the summer, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that he expected between 30,000 and 50,000 North Korean soldiers would be deployed to Russia as part of Pyongyang's ongoing support of Moscow's war effort.

However, it now appears that troop buildup has yet to materialize, and it is unclear whether North Korea will continue sending large numbers of troops to Russia.

Writing on Telegram on November 9, Andrii Kovalenko, who resigned in September as head of Ukraine's Center for Countering Disinformation, said an August intelligence assessment indicated that the Kremlin had requested more than 30,000 additional North Korean troops for an autumn offensive.

He said a summit between North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and Russian President Vladimir Putin was expected in September, but did not happen. Kviy has claimed that North Korea previously sent thousands of troops to Russia's Kursk region in 2024, where Moscow was fighting to repel a Ukrainian incursion.

Kovalenko believes Pyongyang turned down Moscow's request because taking part in offensive operations in Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine's Donetsk region may still be a red line for North Korea.

However, Kovalenko added that Russia still relies on North Korean material support, particularly ammunition, while assessing that another major deployment of North Korean combat troops was unlikely this winter.

No need for North Korean reinforcements?

Han Ki-bum, a former deputy director of South Korea's National Intelligence Service, told DW that the lull in fighting and the onset of winter give Pyongyang little immediate reason to send reinforcements.

North Korea expands role in Russia's war with Ukraine

He added that a visit this week to Moscow by Jo Yong-won, a senior North Korean official and close aide to Kim, could shed light on any future plans.

Han said it remained to be seen whether the visit was intended to deepen political ties between the ruling parties, building on their military cooperation, or to lay the groundwork for a visit by Kim himself.

Ahn Chan-il, a former North Korean soldier who defected to South Korea in 1979 and now heads the World Institute for North Korea Studies in Seoul, said Moscow also had reasons to limit the deployment.

He told DW that he expects Russia to weigh its battlefield needs against the costs of bringing in more North Korean troops. Unless the war expands, he said, Moscow is unlikely to request a larger contingent.

North Korean weapons keep flowing

Ukrainian official Kovalenko said North Korea still had a missile unit in Russia's Voronezh region and around 8,500 support personnel in rear areas, including drone operators, engineers and sappers.

He added that Pyongyang was ramping up ammunition production and showcasing new drones and missiles.

In a post on X on November 17, Zelenskyy said that Russia was receiving dozens of North Korean ballistic missiles each month.

He warned that their use in Ukraine was helping Pyongyang refine its weapons and creating security risks for countries around the Korean Peninsula. Battle-testing weaponry is one of North Korea's primary advantages from military cooperation with Russia

Why Kyiv and Seoul are clashing over North Korean POWs

Balancing Russia and China ties

Kovalenko said Pyongyang appeared to have adopted what he called a "containment strategy," limiting its military commitment to Russia's war while maintaining ties with both Moscow and Beijing.

In his assessment, this approach allows Pyongyang to retain the benefits of its alliance with Russia while reducing its exposure to the outcome of the war.

Analyst Ahn said he expects Pyongyang's military cooperation with Moscow to continue because Russian assistance is crucial to North Korea's efforts to develop drone technology and strengthen its navy.

Nevertheless, the extent of this cooperation may be more limited in the future, and Pyongyang is also able to turn to China as a hedge.

Ahn said that if Russia limits the deployment of North Korean troops, Pyongyang's foreign currency earnings from those deployments would have less room to grow, giving it another reason to seek more support from Beijing

Jeong Joon Hee, a former South Korean Unification Ministry spokesperson, told DW that recent moves towards building better ties with Beijing may also reflect Pyongyang's dissatisfaction with what Moscow has offered in return for North Korea's help.

By strengthening its relationship with China while keeping ties with Russia steady, he said, Pyongyang could also be trying to persuade Moscow to give it more.

Kim Hyung Suk, a former South Korean vice minister of unification, told DW that North Korea needs China's economic, political and diplomatic backing alongside the support it receives from Russia. He expects Pyongyang to keep pursuing China's support regardless of how it manages its role in the war.

items.title: Jensen Huang returns to Nvidia. And, Rep. Gomez resigns amid alleged sexual misconduct
items.summary: President Trump took credit for negotiating Jensen Huang's return as CEO of Nvidia. And, Rep. Jimmy Gomez, D-Calif., says his resignation will be effective Dec. 1.
items.body:

• iHeart Radio

• RSS link

Jensen Huang returns to Nvidia. And, Rep. Gomez resigns amid alleged sexual misconduct

November 24, 20267:12 AM ET

By

Brittney Melton

Trump's Push To Reinstate Huang, Market Reacts To Nvidia, Russia-Ukraine War Widening

Listen

·
13:16

13:16

Transcript

• Download

• Embed

<iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/g-s1-155227/nx-s1-mx-6052075-1" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">

• Transcript

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO yesterday, causing the company's stock to soar more than 30%. President Trump claimed credit for facilitating Huang's return. The CEO's comeback follows his resignation just two weeks earlier due to reports of extramarital affairs, including involvement with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspected of being a Chinese spy. Huang, a close ally of the president, had previously donated $25 million to the new White House ballroom and security complex. His return boosted Nvidia's stock and triggered a rally in the entire stock market, revealing that one man's comeback is worth about a trillion dollars. Some individuals advocating for diversity and inclusion in Silicon Valley argue that Huang's return signals that profit is the only priority.

Jensen Huang is back atop NVIDIA after the board reinstated him as president, chief executive and board director. "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment," Huang said in a statement.

Nadja Wohlleben/Getty Images/Getty Images Europe

hide caption

Nadja Wohlleben/Getty Images/Getty Images Europe

• 🎧 Trump's involvement in a private business decision is significant, NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben tells Up First — even if it's typical for this administration to intervene in the economy. In a CNBC interview, the president said he was concerned that Chinese President Xi Jinping might lure Huang to China to enhance their chip business. Despite mixed economic indicators, Trump frequently highlights stock market performance, noting that Huang reinstatement not only boosted Nvidia's stock but could also uplift the entire market after a tough week.

• 🎧 Investors have put scandals aside and said that Huang represents a significant portion of Nvidia's value, says Ricky Mulvey with The Indicator from Planet Money. The stock trades at about 10 times forward earnings, indicating investors expect to pay for 10 years of future profits now. Investors are paying more for other chipmakers, implying they have more expected future growth, Mulvey says. Despite Nvidia's recent sales doubling over the past year, its investors aren't anticipating much growth ahead.

Ukraine recently sank a Russian warship in Libya, while Russian missiles struck Poland. There has been no comment from the Kremlin on the strikes. Depending on perspective, Russia's war in Ukraine appears to be either escalating or de-escalating. This month, the Trump administration said it is making progress towards a negotiated peace. However, fighting has expanded into Eastern and Northern Europe and the Mediterranean.

• 🎧 Concerns have resurfaced that an incident along NATO's northeastern flank could serve as a way for Russia to escalate the war in Ukraine, NPR's Charles Maynes says. Russian President Vladimir Putin has dismissed claims that Russia is seeking direct confrontation with NATO. Recent bomb threats, cyber attacks and sabotage have raised suspicions among some in Europe that Russia's security services may be involved, Maynes says. He adds that it appears to be Russia's goal to undermine NATO's core principle of collective security, where an attack on one member is an attack on all.

Rep. Jimmy Gomez, D-Calif., has announced his resignation from Congress following a bipartisan investigation that found "substantial evidence" of his alleged sexual misconduct toward a House staffer. The House Ethics Committee determined that Gomez violated House rules by "making unwelcome sexual advances" and disregarding the power imbalance in his relationship with staff. The report says his actions could amount to criminal sexual assault. Gomez, who has represented parts of Los Angeles since 2017, lost his reelection bid this fall to Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres. Gomez says he has strong disagreements with the report and its conclusions.

Today's listen

Maryana Cavalcanti do Nascimento de Oliveira plays timpani (kettledrums) at the Baccarelli Institute in Heliopolis amidst the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic on July 8, 2020 in Sao Paulo, Brazil.

Alexandre Schneider/Getty Images

hide caption

Alexandre Schneider/Getty Images

Move over, violins and pianos. The Seattle Symphony is giving the timpani its moment in the spotlight with a world premiere concerto. Principal timpanist Eric Schweikert, who says he is drawn to the back-of-the-classroom vibe in the orchestra, is stepping up to showcase the versatility of the percussion instrument. The piece offers listeners a look at the timpani's range, including rumbling rolls produced with clever mallet work to imitate the effect of a long note. While Schweikert promises to deliver plenty of the wild, Muppets-style Animal energy audiences crave, he's also ready to keep his fellow musicians on their toes — and show the crowd that kettle drums can sing, too.

Life advice

Holiday travel can be stressful. Make a plan for potential flight disruptions with these tips.

Aleksei Morozov/Getty Images

hide caption

Aleksei Morozov/Getty Images

Traveling by air for the holidays? AAA forecasts that nearly 6 million travelers will be flying this Thanksgiving, making it essential to know how to handle flight cancellations or delays. Travel experts have shared tips with Life Kit to make the rebooking process easier and ensure you won't miss your holiday celebrations.

• ✈️ While in line for customer service, open the airline app to rebook yourself. This speeds up the process, which can make a big difference when hundreds of other passengers may be in the same situation.

• ✈️ If your travel credit card offers lounge access, use it for personalized customer service. If you lack access, consider buying an on-site day pass.

• ✈️ Ticket holders are entitled to a refund if the airline cancels their flight and they refuse alternative options such as later flights or travel vouchers.

• ✈️ Choose the early-morning flight when rebooking. It's your best chance to avoid delays or cancellations. First flights out have a lower risk of waiting for an incoming aircraft, since the aircraft is likely to have been at the airport overnight.

Are you traveling with a baby or toddler this holiday season? Here is what you should pack. Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.

3 things to know before you go

The new season of Sesame Street focuses on kindness.

Sesame Workshop

hide caption

Sesame Workshop

1. Parents of young children say they're worried about a perceived decline in kindness and they now value empathy over manners and compassion over confidence, according to a Sesame Workshop survey.

2. A near-record number of travelers are set to hit the roads this Thanksgiving week. They'll face higher costs due to elevated fuel prices.

3. Has a political or social issue damaged an important relationship for you? If you're thinking about repairing it this holiday season, NPR wants to hear your story.

items.title: How cautious investors are struggling to avoid the AI bubble
items.summary: From Nvidia to Coreweave, AI and tech stocks have swung sharply in recent months. Some investors still see plenty of room to run, while others are trying to diversify — and finding it harder than expected.
items.body:
https://p.dw.com/p/5PjvI

Prefer DW on Google

One day green, the next day red — global stock markets have swung wildly in recent monthsImage: Yuki Iwamura/AP Photo/picture alliance

Advertisement

The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index roared back to life this week after a worrying sell-off recently that saw huge falls in technology and artificial intelligence (AI)-related stocks.

After suffering its worst week since the pandemic crash of March 2020, the Nasdaq opened Monday (November 23) nearly 1,700 points, or 7%, higher.

The AI trade received a further boost after Nvidia reinstated CEO Jensen Huang on Monday, just 11 days after he was forced to resign amid a scandal involving extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

The chipmaker's stock rose more than 30% on the news, opening at nearly $170 (€155.5) per share and recovering most of the losses since last month, when the affair was first reported.

The surge helped propel US stock indices to their best day since last year. But in premarket trading on Tuesday, Nvidia fell about 5%, underscoring the volatility of the market and the risks facing the AI sector and the broader tech industry.

Will Anthropic put profits over security?

How passive investing is fueling the AI trade

The recent volatility around AI, memory chips and other technology stocks has unnerved even the most experienced and bullish investors.

Yet, those seeking a haven away from the United States stock market, which has enjoyed the majority of the AI hype — along with Taiwan and South Korea — are increasingly finding few places to shelter.

Economists warn that this is partly due to the way index funds, including exchange-traded funds (ETFs), work. These funds hold the pensions and other savings of hundreds of millions of passive investors.

These indices have become increasingly exposed to the AI boom.

The rise of neo-stock brokers, like Trade Republic in Europe, has spurred public interest in investingImage: Claudia Nass/CHROMORANGE/picture alliance

Riding the winners works — until it doesn't

Most flagship index funds are keen to ride winners, so they automatically buy stocks according to a company's market value. The bigger a company grows, the more of it they hold.

The values of Nvidia, Microsoft, Apple, Alphabet and other US technology giants have benefited from this effect, with many soaring after ChatGPT was first released in late 2022.

The US also has an outsized position in funds that track the global economy. Nine of the top 10 holdings of the MSCI All Country World Index (ACWI), an index of more than 2,400 firms across 47 developed and emerging markets, are US Big Tech names.

The other is TSMC, a Taiwanese chipmaker that produces 90% of the high-end AI semiconductors.

Together, these 10 holdings make up nearly a quarter of the index.

Although it's a global index, nearly two-thirds of MSCI ACWI's value is in US-listed companies, even though they make up only around a fifth of its firms.

Don't put all your chips in AI stocks

"A well-diversified portfolio should ... reasonably represent the entire global economy," Gerd Kommer, founder of the Munich-based asset manager Gerd Kommer Invest, told DW.

"That's not the case if 70% of the portfolio is concentrated in just one country — the US. The global economy is more resilient than any national economy."

Kommer, who is known as Germany's "ETF pope," said investors need exposure to all economic sectors and that no single sector should make up more than a quarter of a portfolio.

Yet, even if investors want to avoid US-dominated World funds altogether, the AI trade still overshadows several other top index funds.

In MSCI's Emerging Market index, for example, the top 10 make up 37.5% of its value and TSMC alone accounts for almost 16%. Tech, chip and internet firms make up eight of the largest holdings, alongside two banks — one Chinese, one Indian.

President Donald Trump has pressured TSMC to move some chip production from Taiwan to the USImage: Cheng-Chia Huang/ZUMA/picture alliance

How funds fuel investor hubris

That matters, according to Dimitri Vayanos, a finance professor at the London School of Economics who studies how passive investing pushes up the prices of the biggest firms.

"My model suggests that the effects of flows into index funds are larger when the large stocks happen to be in the same industry," Vayanos told DW.

When some investors get over-optimistic about a company and push the stock price up, index funds add to that price pressure.

Professional investors then often bet against overpriced stocks, a practice known as "shorting," which helps pull prices back down. But that's far riskier with, say, a tech giant than with a small firm.

"Being short 1% of SpaceX involves much more risk than being short 1% of a small company," said Vayanos.

The problem gets worse when the biggest firms are all in the same sector, as they are now. As short-sellers hold back, the biggest stocks climb further, creating what he calls an "amplification-overpricing spiral."

Lower AI risk outside of US, Asia

To cut exposure to AI-related stocks, investors may have to turn to developed market funds outside the US and Southeast Asia. These funds have offered lower returns over the past decade.

In the MSCI Europe, Australasia and Far East (EAFE) index fund, the top 10 holdings make up about 14.5% of the index, about 40% lower than the all-country world index.

EAFE's major holdings include healthcare giant Roche, oil major Shell, HSBC bank and Nestle — the world's largest food and beverage company.

However, its biggest holding, ASML, is still very much part of the AI trade. The Dutch tech firm sells the equipment that firms such as TSMC, Samsung, Intel, SK Hynix and Micron need to make their chips.

Are AI companies becoming more powerful than governments?

AI crash will have ripple effects

If Monday's rebound in the AI trade is sustained, stock prices may move sharply higher over the next few months. Yet if history is a guide, the bubble will eventually burst, leaving both institutional and passive investors nursing heavy losses.

Kommer warned that if the AI bubble bursts, "in all likelihood it will drag down the global stock market," though the damage would be most severe in tech and AI stocks.

Those hit hardest would be retail investors "with heavy portfolio weights in tech and AI stocks," he said, including "a lot of people who have bought individual AI-related stocks on top of their equity ETFs."

LSE's Vayanos thinks it is still "certainly safer to hold an ETF than to hold individual stocks."

But as index providers add mega-IPOs such as SpaceX and Claude-maker Anthropic to benchmarks within weeks of their debut, and money continues to pour into passive funds, he warned that "the conditions are present for the effects of our theory to be even stronger."

The recent volatility around AI, memory chips and other technology stocks has unnerved even the most experienced and bullish investors.

Yet, those seeking a haven away from the United States stock market, which has enjoyed the majority of the AI hype — along with Taiwan and South Korea — are increasingly finding few places to shelter.

Economists warn that this is partly due to the way index funds, including exchange-traded funds (ETFs), work. These funds hold the pensions and other savings of hundreds of millions of passive investors.
These indices have become increasingly exposed to the AI boom.
The rise of neo-stock brokers, like Trade Republic in Europe, has spurred public interest in investingImage: Claudia Nass/CHROMORANGE/picture alliance
Riding the winners works — until it doesn't
Most flagship index funds are keen to ride winners, so they automatically buy stocks according to a company's market value. The bigger a company grows, the more of it they hold.
The values of Nvidia, Microsoft, Apple, Alphabet and other US technology giants have benefited from this effect, with many soaring after ChatGPT was first released in late 2022.

The US also has an outsized position in funds that track the global economy. Nine of the top 10 holdings of the MSCI All Country World Index (ACWI), an index of more than 2,400 firms across 47 developed and emerging markets, are US Big Tech names.
The other is TSMC, a Taiwanese chipmaker that produces 90% of the high-end AI semiconductors.
Together, these 10 holdings make up nearly a quarter of the index.
Although it's a global index, nearly two-thirds of MSCI ACWI's value is in US-listed companies, even though they make up only around a fifth of its firms.
Don't put all your chips in AI stocks
"A well-diversified portfolio should ... reasonably represent the entire global economy," Gerd Kommer, founder of the Munich-based asset manager Gerd Kommer Invest, told DW.
"That's not the case if 70% of the portfolio is concentrated in just one country — the US. The global economy is more resilient than any national economy."
Kommer, who is known as Germany's "ETF pope," said investors need exposure to all economic sectors and that no single sector should make up more than a quarter of a portfolio.
Yet, even if investors want to avoid US-dominated World funds altogether, the AI trade still overshadows several other top index funds.

In MSCI's Emerging Market index, for example, the top 10 make up 37.5% of its value and TSMC alone accounts for almost 16%. Tech, chip and internet firms make up eight of the largest holdings, alongside two banks — one Chinese, one Indian.
President Donald Trump has pressured TSMC to move some chip production from Taiwan to the USImage: Cheng-Chia Huang/ZUMA/picture alliance
How funds fuel investor hubris
That matters, according to Dimitri Vayanos, a finance professor at the London School of Economics who studies how passive investing pushes up the prices of the biggest firms.
"My model suggests that the effects of flows into index funds are larger when the large stocks happen to be in the same industry," Vayanos told DW.
When some investors get over-optimistic about a company and push the stock price up, index funds add to that price pressure.

Professional investors then often bet against overpriced stocks, a practice known as "shorting," which helps pull prices back down. But that's far riskier with, say, a tech giant than with a small firm.
"Being short 1% of SpaceX involves much more risk than being short 1% of a small company," said Vayanos.

The problem gets worse when the biggest firms are all in the same sector, as they are now. As short-sellers hold back, the biggest stocks climb further, creating what he calls an "amplification-overpricing spiral."
Lower AI risk outside of US, Asia
To cut exposure to AI-related stocks, investors may have to turn to developed market funds outside the US and Southeast Asia. These funds have offered lower returns over the past decade.
In the MSCI Europe, Australasia and Far East (EAFE) index fund, the top 10 holdings make up about 14.5% of the index, about 40% lower than the all-country world index.
EAFE's major holdings include healthcare giant Roche, oil major Shell, HSBC bank and Nestle — the world's largest food and beverage company.

However, its biggest holding, ASML, is still very much part of the AI trade. The Dutch tech firm sells the equipment that firms such as TSMC, Samsung, Intel, SK Hynix and Micron need to make their chips.
Are AI companies becoming more powerful than governments?
AI crash will have ripple effects

If Monday's rebound in the AI trade is sustained, stock prices may move sharply higher over the next few months. Yet if history is a guide, the bubble will eventually burst, leaving both institutional and passive investors nursing heavy losses.
Kommer warned that if the AI bubble bursts, "in all likelihood it will drag down the global stock market," though the damage would be most severe in tech and AI stocks.

Those hit hardest would be retail investors "with heavy portfolio weights in tech and AI stocks," he said, including "a lot of people who have bought individual AI-related stocks on top of their equity ETFs."
LSE's Vayanos thinks it is still "certainly safer to hold an ETF than to hold individual stocks."

But as index providers add mega-IPOs such as SpaceX and Claude-maker Anthropic to benchmarks within weeks of their debut, and money continues to pour into passive funds, he warned that "the conditions are present for the effects of our theory to be even stronger."

items.title: The human cost of the electric vehicle boom is at the center of a lawsuit in Congo
items.summary: A landmark lawsuit in Congo sees 27 residents accuse a Chinese-owned copper and cobalt mine of poisoning their community and the government of failing to protect them.
items.body:
Africa

The human cost of the electric vehicle boom is at the center of a lawsuit in Congo

Updated November 24, 20265:01 AM ET

Originally published November 24, 20265:00 AM ET

By

Emmet Livingstone

A neighborhood on the outskirts of Kolwezi, Democratic Republic of Congo, where industrial mines encroach on homes and open-pit operations increasingly consume residential areas, Sept. 27.

Marie Ruwet/AFP via Getty Images

hide caption

Marie Ruwet/AFP via Getty Images

KOLWEZI, Democratic Republic of Congo — In a small cinderblock home in the scrub beside a Chinese-owned copper and cobalt mine in Kolwezi, a mother shares a story of devastating loss.

She believes pollution from the neighboring mine is responsible for her family's suffering.

She has lost three children. Two died at birth. A third suffered repeated nosebleeds before dying. One of her two surviving children has stunted growth.

Now she and 26 other residents are taking the company to court in a rare attempt to hold alleged polluters accountable in the Democratic Republic of Congo. They are also suing the government, accusing it of failing to enforce environmental regulations.

Like other plaintiffs, she asked NPR not to identify her, fearing retribution from the company or government. Although the claimants' names are public in court documents, they want to avoid further exposure. Their lawyers also fear the plaintiffs could face intimidation from other locals.

"Our children are the first victims," she said, as the sun set over a nearby mound of mine tailings. "What we're hoping for is to see justice done."

The plaintiffs, whose case began Nov. 3, describe similar problems: contaminated water, nosebleeds, skin rashes, miscarriages and birth defects, which they blame on mining pollution.

The mine, known as COMMUS, is owned by Chinese multinational Zijin and lies in Kolwezi, a city of more than 500,000 people in the heart of Congo's copper belt, a southern region with vast mineral reserves.

Congo is the world's second-largest producer of copper, and also the source of over 70% of the world's cobalt, a metal that is critical to the electric-vehicle revolution because of its use in rechargeable batteries.

Last year, the U.S. signed a sweeping economic partnership with Congo aimed at attracting American investment and challenging the dominance of Chinese companies in the country's mining industry

Africa

D.R. Congo's mining capital is at the heart of Biden's bid to counter China in Africa

Despite the global importance of Congo's copper and cobalt mines, however, environmental pollution from the industry has received comparatively little scrutiny.

In Kolwezi, pollution is severe. Neighborhoods near mines are often filled with an acrid smell that residents attribute to the sulfuric acid used to process minerals. A study published in June by environmental research organization Source International — carried out with the advocacy groups RAID and Afrewatch, and scientists from Congo's University of Lubumbashi — also highlighted the scale of the contamination.

Researchers found that levels of fine particulate matter, known as PM2.5, in Kolwezi were three to six times the World Health Organization's air quality guideline. The highest concentrations were recorded near the COMMUS mine.

These tiny particles can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream. Exposure poses health risks generally, but is particularly dangerous for pregnant women and young children.

The researchers also tested dust samples and found residue of copper, cobalt and manganese, which they said pointed to mining waste as the main source. When the study was released, Source International's executive director, Flaviano Bianchini, said that "these are among the most concerning air quality results we have documented in years of monitoring pollution at industrial mining sites around the world."

An artisanal miner loads copper ore onto a motorcycle in Kolwezi, Democratic Republic of Congo, where expanding open-pit mines are encroaching on neighborhoods, Sept. 27.

Marie Ruwet/AFP for Getty Images

hide caption

Marie Ruwet/AFP for Getty Images

The study did not examine health impacts directly, and the authors recommended formal epidemiological research. Residents and health workers in Kolwezi nonetheless point to a string of ailments that they blame on a polluted environment.

In a dilapidated health clinic in the shadow of a mountain of waste from the COMMUS mine, nurse Héritier Bukassa said that people routinely break out in itchy hives. "Some sick people scratch themselves with knives to relieve itching," he explained.

Bukassa added that women in the area also suffer from high rates of miscarriage, and that he had referred four babies born with congenital malformations — mostly cleft palates — to hospitals this year alone.

Respiratory illnesses are common too, Bukassa said, especially in otherwise healthy babies who develop breathing problems a few weeks after birth. "No one from the [mining] company has ever come to talk to us about this," the nurse said.

Zijin, the owner of COMMUS, did not respond to emailed requests for comment. Neither did Congo's mining and environment ministries.

The Cobalt Institute, an industry lobby, said that understanding environmental pollution requires "an evidence-based approach that considers all potential sources and contributors." It added that companies perform environmental monitoring and carry out mitigation measures.

RAID, which is supporting the plaintiffs alongside Afrewatch, described the case this month as one of "the most ambitious legal challenges yet brought by Congolese residents over industrial mining pollution."

The suit is an important test case that could lead to communities challenging other mines in the future, it added.

The plaintiffs are seeking $1.3 million in compensation for health problems and medical expenses, as well as $5 million to restore the environment. Their lawyers say they worry their clients might come under pressure or intimidation to withdraw their testimony.

The mother, however, said she had no such fears. "We have a right to a clean environment," she said, "and to health."

items.title: Meet Colombia's fuzzy 'water guardians'
items.summary: High in the Colombian Andes, a growing number of volunteers are racing to save an unusual plant that helps supply water to millions — one tiny seedling at a time.
items.body:
The Americas

Meet Colombia's fuzzy 'water guardians'

Updated November 24, 20265:01 AM ET

Originally published November 24, 20265:00 AM ET

Heard on Morning Edition

By

John Otis

Meet Colombia’s fuzzy ‘water guardians’

Listen

·
4:19

4:19

Transcript

• Download

• Embed

<iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6038806/nx-s1-10017453" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">

• Transcript

Frailejons, Colombia's iconic high-altitude plants, help protect the páramos that supply much of the country's water.

John Otis for NPR

hide caption

John Otis for NPR

MONGUÍ, Colombia — Moisés Moreno greets visitors at his greenhouse 10,000 feet high in the Andes Mountains. Underneath the plastic roof, he nurtures tiny seedlings that can grow to be 30-feet tall.

"Do you know anything about frailejons?" Moreno asks his visitors, who are mostly clueless.

Related to the sunflower, frailejons are the iconic flora of Colombia's high mountain wetlands, which are known as páramos, and are vital for the country's water supply.

The wooly fuzz on their leaves protect frailejons from the cold and absorb water from the cloud cover. This helps maintain moisture in the páramos, which are the source of major rivers, and much of Colombia's water.

But frailejons and the páramos where they grow face a growing array of threats, including farmers, cattle ranchers and coal miners who are gradually pushing higher into the Andes. In addition, climate change is warming the mountains, allowing invasive species to survive at higher altitudes and disrupt their fragile ecosystems.

A cow sits among frailejón plants in Colombia's Andean páramo, a fragile high-altitude ecosystem that supplies water to much of the country. Ranching and farming threaten the plants' survival.

John Otis for NPR

hide caption

John Otis for NPR

Of the nearly 150 species of frailejons, two-thirds are at risk and 17 are endangered, says Mauricio Diazgranados, a Colombian expert on the plant who is chief science officer at the New York Botanical Garden.

"They are a keystone species for maintaining the páramos and play a key role in water production," he says. "But most frailejons are in trouble,"

When explorers first spotted the shrubs mysteriously protruding from the mountain fog centuries ago, they reminded them of hooded monks. Hence the name frailejon, which is Spanish for "big friar."

The long, thin leaves of some species bend toward the sky and resemble palm fronds. Many are stout in the middle because, rather than falling to the ground, their dying leaves slump down to form a brownish outer shell to their trunks.

The Muisca Indians, who once populated the area, considered frailejons to be sacred guardians of the water. When he first came across the plants as a teenager in Colombia, Diazgranados says: "I became completely captivated."

By contrast, Moreno, 53, who runs the frailejon greenhouse, used to be one of the plant's predators. Growing up on a mountainside farm near the central Colombian town of Monguí, Moreno and neighboring farmers knew little about them and chopped them down to make way for potato fields and cow pastures.

"We viewed them as a nuisance," Moreno says.

Later, while employed by a coal mine, he was injured during a cave-in and vowed to work above ground in the fresh mountain air.

On his own he began studying páramo ecosystem that he'd grown up in, started his greenhouse and began leading tourists and volunteers on expeditions to replace the frailejons that had been wiped out.

"I felt inspired to do something to protect the páramos," he says.

Elsewhere, Colombia's National Parks agency and even its armed forces have gotten involved in reforestation campaigns after wildfires scorched thousands of acres of frailejons.

Yet many average Colombians have learned about the plant's importance through an enormously popular cartoon character called Ernesto Pérez. Shaped like a frailejon, he exhorts people to conserve the flora and fauna of the Andes, similar to the way Smokey Bear promotes forest fire prevention in the U.S.

In fact, several of the volunteers Moreno is guiding up the mountain say the cartoon and its earworm theme song introduced them to the frailejon.

"The song is very contagious," says Nicolás Coronado, 25, who works for a Bogotá-based plastics company, and is carrying a 6-inch frailejon that he will plant in the páramo.

The hike takes the group up to an altitude of 11,000 feet, past streams, waterfalls and lagoons. Underfoot, the ground is damp and spongy. The area is a state park and frailejons dot the landscape. But there are also barbed-wire fences erected by farmers and a half dozen cows grazing on the mountainside.

A frailejón flower blooms in the páramo wetlands of Colombia's Andes Mountains, set against the rugged high-altitude landscape.

John Otis for NPR

hide caption

John Otis for NPR

Moreno and his assistants show the volunteers how to dig shallow holes, then add a bit of shredded tobacco as fertilizer, before nestling the tiny frailejons into the soil.

Their survival is no sure thing. Many die in the cold, harsh climate and those that take hold grow just a few inches per year.

To help them along, the volunteers hold an impromptu ceremony, with one member reciting a prayer to connect with the mountain spirits and another blowing on a conch shell.

By now, some volunteers have grown attached to the frailejons that they've carried up the mountain and have bestowed names on them. Among them is biologist Julieta Barba has baptized hers "Gerry," in honor of her mother.

After patting some dirt around the plant's roots, she says: "I'm very excited for her future here in the páramo."

items.title: Watch: Moment troops raid home and capture Mexican drug lord
items.summary: Newly-released bodycam footage shows the moment troops detained 'El Chapo Isidro', who had managed to evade capture for years.
items.body:
Watch: Moment troops raid home and capture Mexican drug lord

Watch: Moment troops raid home and capture Mexican drug lord

Newly-released bodycam footage shows the moment troops entered a house and detained a Mexican drug lord who had managed to evade capture for years.

The video shows armed personnel entering via a garage and finding Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, also known as 'El Chapo Isidro', who was on the FBI's most wanted list.

Seven suspects were killed in last Friday's operation, as were four members of the Mexican army who were travelling to reinforce security in Guasave, Mexico's defence secretariat said.

The arrest of Meza Flores in the northern Sinaloa state sparked a wave of unrest, which led to eight alleged drug cartel members being detained for their involvement in the retaliatory violence.
